messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
parts:
Hi, 

I read various post about contraints, and come up to the idea to 
use Lagrange Multipliers in STAN. See example 1 in:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier

I came up with the following basic model:

data {
}
parameters {
  real x;
  real y;
  real la;
}
model {
 // x  ~ normal(0,100);
//  y  ~ normal(0,100);
//  la ~ normal(0,100);
 
  increment_log_prob(-square(x+y+la*(square(x)+square(y)-1)));
  //increment_log_prob(-0.5*square(1+2*la*x));
  //increment_log_prob(-0.5*square(1+2*la*y));
//  increment_log_prob(-0.5*square(square(x)+square(y)-1));
}

I go several warnings:

Warning messages:
1: There were 27 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help. 
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
 
> x<-mean(extract(fit,"x")$x)
> y<-mean(extract(fit,"y")$y)
> la<-mean(extract(fit,"la")$la)
> la
[1] 0.609033
> x
[1] -0.0002591018
> y
[1] 0.06798691

The solution is not correct. Well, I didn't expected that it would work.
STAN makes use of autodiff, thus I would hope someone has an idea. 

André

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
parts:
I don't understand

1. what the inference problem is (the wikipedia example is an
optimization problem),

2. how you mean to apply Lagrange multipliers for your problem (once you
describe it to us),

3. what you are trying to do in Stan.

What you have below is a function that is quadratic in x and y and
linear in la. This is not a proper posterior, as it is not even
bounded, so Stan of course cannot sample from it --- no algorithm could,
as it is not a density of a distribution.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
parts:
Tam, Bob, everybody,

I was into coding a bayesian support vector machine (bSVM) in STAN. In their dual form
in common to use lagrange multiplier to cope with the inequality condition. 

I looked in the group here and thought maybe somebody else know how to handle
contraints. I found:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/CFbIiXAzHl0/mSRKER0WNcoJ

So I tried to make it very simple and put the lagrange example in the STAN optimizer. 
You all right. I doesn't makes sense. 

Just for informational background:
 
I have had the idea to use STAN as an Bayesian optimizer. 
Currently we do optimizing like an optimizing tunnel. 
We pick on point, optimize and get one result.  
We do that repeatedly. At the end of the other side
we get a 'picture'.
But what, if we could transmit whole distributions 
through the "tunnel"? 
Our solver have constraints. So how could I had constraints
to STAN. Thus I come up with the Lagrange multiplier idea. 
To make it more practical, in the company I worked before,
we had a simulation of the factory. We did a simulation,
picked one state out of the simulation process, optimized
that. Repeated that n-times and then at the end we 
reviewed the optimized points.

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
parts:
I don't know much about either Lagrange multipliers or Bayesian
optimization. Stan is only able to do MCMC, variational inference,
and optimization.

Constraints on variables need to be implemented in Stan through transfroms
from R^N to a suitable natural space for modeling (usually a constrained
portion of R^M, for M >= N). An example is mapping any point in R^N to a
simplex in R^(N+1) using softmax (we use a stick-breaking construction, but
the idea's the same).

- Bob

messages.author: 37f85c6188fe5eeb
messages.subject: Re: Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
parts:
On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 1:41:03 PM UTC-7, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
Hi, 

I read various post about contraints, and come up to the idea to 
use Lagrange Multipliers in STAN. See example 1 in:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier

Lagrange multipliers are more or less an analytic technique (ie. if you are trying to solve analytically for locations where derivatives vanish), they aren't necessarily appropriate directly for numerical usage.  A related technique is "penalty" methods. If you are willing to put up with "soft" constraints g(x) \approx 0, you can take f(x) + K*(g(x))^2. The contribution from g(x) is obviously is minimized when g(x) = 0. When K goes to infinity the solution to this penalized minimization procedure is equal to the constrained minimum of f(x) subject to g(x)=0. But this is not always a practically effective method.
